access.edition_or_version: Latin text with English translation, Loeb Classical Library 91, ed. and trans. Susanna Braund (Harvard University Press, 2004); standard commentary: Braund, Satires Book 1 (CUP, 1996)

mechanics.premise: Six books of first-person verse satire cataloguing the vices of Rome — patrons and patronage, ambition, sexual commerce, urban squalor — through a speaker who measures the city against standards it keeps betraying.
mechanics.point_of_view: Sustained first-person satiric persona addressing the reader directly, staging encounters and apostrophizing targets; the speaker is a constructed voice, not a transparent author.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Catalogue and enumeration; abrupt mimetic scenes dropped into argument; grotesque exaggeration; rhetorical questions and apostrophe; moralized indignant diction throughout.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Wry setup -> accumulating outrage -> full invective -> oblique withdrawal, with the speaker repeatedly vowing to stop and returning.
mechanics.dialogue: Reported and staged confrontations; the persona argues with patrons, devotees, and fellow travellers as if cornering them in the street.
mechanics.conventions: Foundational text of the Western satiric tradition and the origin of the term Juvenalian for moral-indictment satire.
tone_mechanisms: moralized indignation at stated versus actual standards
mechanics.critical_reception: Transmitted through medieval and Renaissance schools; became a school text and a standing model for English satire (Donne, Johnson, Swift).
mechanics.verification_note: Existence, authorship, and dating (first book c. 100-101; final surviving book after 127) confirmed via Wikipedia API extract (Juvenal) on 2026-09-24; edition identity via publisher and library catalog metadata; mode cross-checked against the repository's satirical-literature genre file. Technique described from standard accounts; no passage reproduced.
